summary:
South Sulawesi stands under Indonesia's national framework, which is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level provisions targeting morality. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

A trans traveller died in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy now frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing directly to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Within that framework, South Sulawesi is one of the eight provinces analysed in OutRight Action International's "Creeping Criminalisation" mapping, which documents how provincial and city bylaws criminalise same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity under regional autonomy.

Makassar has been a recurring site of an anti-LGBT bylaw push since at least early 2023, when the city's draft regulation entered the 2023 local legislative programme as a priority for discussion. Two DPRD Makassar members, including PKS-faction member Azwar ST, said the proposal models itself on Perda already passed elsewhere such as Bogor. Constitutional-law expert Bivitri Susanti called such drafts a trend ahead of the political year that risks worsening discrimination and persecution of LGBT people, and noted that the central government does little to stop discriminatory local regulations.

On 27 April 2025, Makassar mayor Munafri 'Appi' Arifuddin reaffirmed his commitment to pushing through an anti-LGBT Perda after a same-sex act at a night entertainment venue went viral. The deputy chair of the DPRD Makassar law-drafting body, Anwar Faruq, voiced support, saying such a regulation is urgently needed to preserve moral order and religious norms.

As of 25 April 2026, the local rule remains a draft (Ranperda) rather than an enacted regulation. The Makassar city government's women's-empowerment and child-protection agency (DP3A) is intensifying LGBT "prevention" through socialisation and education aimed at school-age children alongside case handling, with counselling and a safe house for reported individuals. DP3A head Ita Isdiana Anwar says most reports come from worried families; DPRD Kota Makassar member Muchlis Misbah, citing a Komisi D monitoring meeting showing rising LGBT numbers alongside HIV/AIDS cases, backs the pending Ranperda on HIV/AIDS and LGBT as legal reinforcement.

Available sources record no enacted Perda with specified penalties for South Sulawesi or Makassar, and no mass police raid or wave of violence against trans people documented in the province.
tangentialFactors:
The pressure in South Sulawesi is administrative and legislative rather than penal at provincial level, which distinguishes it from Aceh, where Sharia punishments reach visitors directly, and from the national level, where the 2022 penal code and the October 2025 presidential decree set the operative risk.

The province's position on the map reflects an active legislative push in a major domestic-tourism gateway, raising the probability of future discriminatory enforcement rather than recording present penal exposure. The score remains above West Sumatra (0.11), where a Perda with articles specifying penalties has already been adopted.

Recurrence matters for expectation-setting: Makassar's draft has been retabled across at least three separate cycles, in 2023 as a prolegda priority, in 2025 with mayoral backing, and in 2026 still pending, so a visitor's exposure is likely to shift with local political calendars rather than with any single announcement.

The Bogor Perda is cited by Makassar legislators as the model, and Bogor is the jurisdiction associated with the June 2025 villa raid that produced 75 arrests, so a bylaw of the kind being drafted has a documented enforcement analogue elsewhere in Indonesia.

Legal scholars quoted in the reporting attribute the persistence of such drafts to weak central oversight; Bivitri Susanti states that the central government does little to stop discriminatory local regulations, which means the national framework does not reliably constrain provincial or municipal initiatives.

The linkage drawn between LGBT figures and HIV/AIDS in the Makassar monitoring reporting provides the public-health rationale used to justify the pending draft, and mirrors the framing behind the national October 2025 security decree.
localsOnly:
Residents of Makassar are the direct subjects of the city's prevention apparatus. DP3A runs socialisation and education sessions aimed at school-age children, handles incoming community reports, and maintains counselling services and a safe house for individuals reported to the agency.

The agency head, Ita Isdiana Anwar, states that most reports originate from worried families, so the reporting channel runs through the household rather than through police or courts.

Residents also face legislative exposure: DPRD Kota Makassar member Muchlis Misbah, referencing a Komisi D monitoring meeting, links rising LGBT numbers to HIV/AIDS cases and argues that the pending Ranperda on HIV/AIDS and LGBT would function as legal reinforcement.

Local legislators have publicly committed to the draft. Mayor Munafri 'Appi' Arifuddin reaffirmed the push in April 2025, and Bapemperda deputy chair Anwar Faruq framed it as necessary to preserve moral order and religious norms.

OutRight Action International's mapping treats South Sulawesi as one of eight provinces where regional autonomy has produced bylaws criminalising same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity, so residents operate under sustained scrutiny from both provincial and city instruments.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Makassar Ranperda on HIV/AIDS and LGBT has been enacted after 25 April 2026 is unresolved; the most recent sourced statement in the inventory still describes it as pending.

No source in the inventory specifies the penalties, if any, that the Makassar draft would attach to same-sex conduct or gender nonconformity, so the severity of the proposed local regime is not sourced.

Whether South Sulawesi has its own provincial-level Perda targeting LGBT people, as distinct from the Makassar city draft, is not sourced; the inventory documents the province only through OutRight's inclusion in its eight-province mapping.

No source records enforcement against trans people in South Sulawesi under a local bylaw, nor any raid of the Puncak type within the province, so the practical consequences of the pending draft for a trans visitor remain unverified.

The connection between the October 2025 presidential decree and any vigilante or security action inside South Sulawesi is not sourced; the August 2026 reporting on vigilante attacks does not identify the provinces concerned.

The circumstances of Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla's death remain contested: his mother alleges police beat him and Indonesian police deny that violence was used, and no adjudicated finding is available in the inventory.
